beliefs.proposition: In E1 hall assemblies the record-keeper's office binds each accepted claim into the hall's cord-record, and only a claim bound there can be pressed against a house; speaking a claim aloud merely announces the binding. The speaker attributes all decisive force to the bound record and none to the spoken announcement.
beliefs.speaker: a retired E1 hall usher, as quoted in the fictional Ushers' Miscellany (in-world oral account)

beliefs.proposition: In the same E1 hall the cord-bindings are only tallies of what the hall has paid out, consulted to check arithmetic and nothing more; a claim becomes binding when the voice-of-the-record office speaks it aloud before the assembly, and the record chest never decides anything. The speaker attributes all decisive force to the spoken claim and none to the binding.
beliefs.speaker: an itinerant E1 tally-reader who worked the same hall's market days, as quoted in the opposing account of the same fictional miscellany (in-world oral account)

symbols.audience: adult E1 members of the hall admitted to the record chest while a dispute is heard
symbols.display_label: Bound-cord knot set on the record chest (sign of the record-keeper's office)
symbols.reading: Inside the E1 hall only, a set of three bound cord-knots fixed to the chest lid marks the chest as the record-keeper's office and tells admitted assembly members that the bindings may be consulted in the dispute being heard; the mark has no defined meaning outside that hall and era, and this drill assigns it no colour and no universal meaning.

symbols.audience: adult E1 members of the hall present when claims are spoken aloud in assembly
symbols.display_label: Plain ring on the speaker's post (sign of the voice-of-the-record office)
symbols.reading: Inside the E1 hall only, a plain uncoloured ring hung on the speaker's post marks the post from which the voice-of-the-record office speaks claims aloud during that assembly; the ring denotes nothing outside that hall and era, and this drill assigns it no colour, no cross-era meaning and no universal meaning.
